name: Luykas Van Alen House

location.text: 2589 New York State Route 9H, Kinderhook, Columbia County, New York

dates.altered: The survey: 'The existing front doer replaces the original which, according to the present owner 3 had a transom above it of two rows of small glass panes. The present entrance porch and the east domers are a comparatively recent addition.' (The stray '3' is what the page prints and is restored here; this note had silently replaced it with a comma, while survey.quotes[1] carries the same sentence verbatim.) Wikipedia adds that the third room was added about 1750 and that some interior features, notably the staircase, 'have been brought in from similar period houses'.
dates.note: THE BUILDER IS DISPUTED AND THE DISPUTE IS ON THE FACE OF THE ARCHIVE. The HABS data page is headed 'THE ADAM VAN ALEN HOUSE' and says the house 'was built in 1737 by either Adam Van Alen (1703-1784) or his fathers Johannes'; the Library's own item line for the same survey carries 'National Register of Historic Places NRIS Number: 67000011', which is the Luykas Van Alen House's number, and the survey's owner, 'Mrs. W*V.A. Herriek', is the Herrick family Wikipedia names as the last Van Alen occupants of the Luykas house. The Columbia County Historical Society and the National Historic Landmark designation call it the Luykas Van Alen House, built circa 1737. Recorded as two names for what the archive joins as one building; neither source is edited.

quotes.text: This house, situated on what was the original Albany Post Road, was built in 1737 by either Adam Van Alen (1703-1784) or his fathers Johannes. The south end of the present house, consisting of two rooms with a fire-place in each, was erected first, the north extension being added later. The existing front doer replaces the original which, according to the present owner 3 had a transom above it of two rows of small glass panes. The present entrance porch and the east domers are a comparatively recent addition.

note: Tranche 2, the Dutch trunk in America. Added by this pass; the two nodes had no brick rural house among their exemplars and this is the one everybody reproduces. TWO POINTS OF FRICTION WORTH KEEPING. (1) `hudson-valley-dutch` says the towns build in brick and the country in stone; the survey records the most famous rural Hudson house of all as 'Brick; stone base'. (2) The survey's account of growth -- two rooms with a fireplace in each, the north extension added later -- is the additive bent-by-bent plan the node describes, and the entrance porch and dormers are recorded as modern, which is worth knowing before reading a photograph of this house as evidence about porches or dormers.
